tagline: Coastal dunes, lagoon banks, and a shipwreck preserved beneath the sea
intro: The Indian River Lagoon–Treasure Coast Scenic Highway follows two different shore-side settings: A1A beside the Atlantic on the barrier island, and US 1 through Fort Pierce and Port St. Lucie on the mainland. Florida Scenic Highways highlights the corridor’s coastal dunes and mangrove-covered lagoon banks, presenting the drive as an introduction to St. Lucie County’s historical, cultural and environmental resources. The byway organization also identifies beaches, a marina and museums as features along the scenic highway.

The 42-mile corridor received its scenic-highway designation on December 14, 2005. By then, preservation had given an offshore wreck a new role: Urca de Lima, lost in 1715, became Florida’s first Underwater Archaeological Preserve in 1987. After decades of salvage permits, Fort Pierce’s city council chose to protect the wreck, and archaeologists examined and mapped it in 1985.

Traveling south, A1A runs the length of North Hutchinson Island, with the Navy UDT-SEAL Museum just south of Pepper Park Beachside. Fort Pierce is the corridor’s central axis. On the southern island, Seaway Drive and the South Bridge connect A1A with US 1; A1A continues as South Ocean Drive. Off Hutchinson Island, the Douglass Beach archaeological site preserves a Spanish wreck above an older land surface.

moments.title: Urca de Lima
moments.text: Urca de Lima lies 200 yards offshore from Jack Island Park, north of Fort Pierce Inlet. Although part of the 1715 Treasure Fleet, the ship carried mostly goods such as cowhides, chocolate and vanilla, along with private silver. Grounded with its hull intact after the hurricane, it supplied provisions to survivors. After salvaging the cargo, the Spanish burned it to the waterline to conceal its position from pirates and privateers. Archaeologists examined and mapped the wreck in 1985, before the preserve was established. The wreck became Florida’s first Underwater Archaeological Preserve in 1987.

moments.title: National Navy UDT-SEAL Museum
moments.text: Demolition-training obstacles from before the Normandy landings are part of the museum’s collection. The original Navy frogmen trained outside Fort Pierce, and veterans helped create the museum by gathering their wartime artifacts and experiences. The effort began at Albert Stankie’s home and grew into a dedicated facility that opened in 1985. Alongside the wartime material are spacecraft training devices used by recovery teams during the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo missions. The collection also includes SEAL delivery vehicles that flood inside, requiring their operators to wear compressed-air tanks. A bronze SEAL figure stands at the center of the museum’s memorial, surrounded by black granite panels bearing the names of the dead.
moments.notice: The collection includes original obstacles used to practice demolition before the Normandy landings.

moments.title: Douglass Beach
moments.text: Off Douglass Beach, a Spanish shipwreck overlies the remains of an older land surface. The underwater site lies off Hutchinson Island in water no deeper than six meters. Pleistocene horse remains, pottery, shell tools and evidence of wetland plants have been recovered there. These finds come from beneath the wreckage of the fleet caught in the 1715 hurricane. Before these discoveries, archaeologists had thought older terrestrial sites would survive only in places where wave action was low. Douglass Beach’s preserved layers helped change that understanding, extending the search to places near barrier islands.
